statements: The chief complaint is a slowly enlarging right neck mass present for 1 year in a 32-year-old man.
The patient’s concern is a persistent submandibular-region mass rather than pain, infection, or systemic illness.
The chronic time course and lack of other symptoms suggest a benign, slow-growing soft tissue or salivary-region neoplasm rather than an acute inflammatory process.
Salient positive findings include a soft, slightly movable mass in the right submandibular region.
Salient positive findings include normal overlying skin.
Salient positive findings include an otherwise unremarkable physical examination.
CT showed a well-defined 5 × 3 cm mixed-density lesion adjacent to the right submandibular gland.
Image segmentation suggested that the lesion contains fat, connective tissue, and osteoid.
That combination strongly points toward a mesenchymal tumor with adipose and osseous/chondroid differentiation.
The lesion is well circumscribed and clinically mobile.
The lesion’s well-circumscribed and clinically mobile nature supports a benign process.
Pertinent negatives include no mention of pain.
Pertinent negatives include no mention of tenderness.
Pertinent negatives include no mention of rapid growth.
Pertinent negatives include no mention of skin changes.
Pertinent negatives include no mention of ulceration.
Pertinent negatives include no mention of cranial nerve deficits.
Pertinent negatives include no mention of constitutional symptoms.
Pertinent negatives include no mention of other abnormal examination findings.
These negatives make infectious lymphadenitis less likely.
These negatives make aggressive salivary malignancy less likely.
These negatives make metastatic nodal disease less likely.
There is no history suggesting congenital presentation.
That lack of congenital history somewhat argues against teratoma.
Adult teratomas can occur.
Pleomorphic adenoma of the submandibular gland is a reasonable initial consideration.
The mass is in the submandibular region.
The mass is slow growing.
The mass is well defined.
The mass appears clinically benign.
Pleomorphic adenoma can contain myxochondroid stromal elements.
Pleomorphic adenoma may appear heterogeneous on imaging.
The lesion is described as adjacent to the submandibular gland rather than clearly arising within it.
The imaging segmentation specifically identified fat, connective tissue, and osteoid.
A substantial fat component is not typical for pleomorphic adenoma.
A substantial fat component makes pleomorphic adenoma less fitting overall.
Teratoma can produce a mixed-density mass containing fat and calcified or osseous elements.
The imaging composition fits teratoma.
Cervical teratomas are much more typical in infants and children.
Adult cervical teratomas are uncommon.
The case provides no additional features of a complex congenital germ cell tumor beyond mixed tissue density.
Teratoma remains plausible.
Teratoma is less likely than a benign adipocytic tumor with osseous/chondroid metaplasia.
Osteo/chondroid lipoma fits especially well.
These rare benign lipomatous tumors are well circumscribed.
These rare benign lipomatous tumors are composed of mature adipose tissue with chondroid and/or osseous matrix.
The CT suggestion of fat, connective tissue, and osteoid is highly characteristic.
The soft, slightly movable, slow-growing nature over 1 year supports a benign lipomatous lesion.
The submandibular region is an unusual but recognized soft tissue location for such a tumor.
The decisive feature is the lesion composition on imaging.
The lesion composition on imaging is fat plus osteoid/connective tissue in a well-defined benign-appearing neck mass.
Among the listed differentials, osteo/chondroid lipoma best integrates the adipose and osseous/chondroid elements.
Among the listed differentials, osteo/chondroid lipoma matches the indolent clinical behavior.
Pleomorphic adenoma explains the location but not the fat-rich composition as well.
Teratoma explains mixed tissues but is less typical in this adult presentation.
The most likely diagnosis is osteochondrolipoma (osteo/chondroid lipoma).
Differential diagnoses include osteo/chondroid lipoma with high likelihood.
Differential diagnoses include pleomorphic adenoma of the submandibular gland with medium likelihood.
Differential diagnoses include teratoma with low likelihood.
The final diagnosis is osteochondrolipoma.
